question: In transfer learning, which part of a pretrained classifier is usually replaced for the new task?
options: The first convolution
The batch normalization layers
The head (final classification layer)
Nothing is replaced
explanation: The head maps features to the source classes. The new task has different classes, so it gets a new head on top of the reused backbone.

question: When does pretraining usually help the most?
options: When the target task has very few labeled examples
When the target task has millions of labels
When source and target tasks are unrelated
When the model is very small
explanation: With scarce labels, a from-scratch model cannot learn good features, so reused features give the largest gain.

question: Why does fine-tuning use a smaller learning rate for the backbone than for the new head?
options: Because the backbone has fewer parameters
Because the backbone's weights are already useful and large updates would destroy them, while the head starts random
Because PyTorch requires it
Because a smaller learning rate makes training faster
explanation: The head needs large steps to go from random to useful; the pretrained backbone only needs small adjustments.

question: Why does set_frozen also call module.eval() on the frozen backbone?
options: To make the forward pass deterministic with dropout only
Because requires_grad=False is ignored otherwise
To move the module to the CPU
Because batch norm keeps updating its running statistics in training mode even when its parameters are frozen
explanation: Running mean and variance are buffers updated in every training-mode forward pass, independently of requires_grad.

question: What is the purpose of the 'random probe' baseline in the lesson?
options: To show that linear heads cannot learn anything
To check that the linear probe's advantage comes from pretrained features, not merely from training a linear head on any frozen CNN
To speed up training
To measure overfitting on the source task
explanation: Random convolutional features are already somewhat useful. Comparing against them isolates the contribution of pretraining.

question: With 30 labels per class, scratch matched fine-tuning and beat the linear probe. What explains this?
options: With enough target data, a model can learn suitable features itself, while frozen features tuned for the source classes cannot adapt
Pretrained models always get worse with more data
The linear probe overfits more than the scratch model
It is a bug in the evaluation
explanation: The benefit of pretraining shrinks as target data grows. Frozen features become the bottleneck; fine-tuning removes it.
